name: Integrated Data Store
tagline: Charles Bachman's 1964 network DBMS at GE: the first direct-access database and the template for CODASYL.
description: Integrated Data Store (IDS) was built by Charles Bachman at General Electric's computer division and released in 1964 for the GE 235. It is generally regarded as the first direct-access database management system: records lived on disk and programs navigated between them through owner-member sets, rather than reading sequential tape files. That navigational network model became the basis of the CODASYL Data Base Task Group standard, and B.F. Goodrich's rewrite of IDS turned into IDMS, which is still sold today. Honeywell carried IDS forward after buying GE's computer business, with IDS/II following in 1975. Bachman received the 1973 Turing Award largely for this work. Nobody runs IDS itself now; it matters as history and as the ancestor of IDMS.
statusNote: Historical system (GE 1964, Honeywell IDS/II from 1975); no longer offered. Its design survives in CA/Broadcom IDMS.

pricing.notes: Originally bundled with GE hardware; IDS/II (1975) became a separately chargeable Honeywell product. Not available today.

strengths: First DBMS to give programs shared, direct access to records on disk
Introduced the owner-member set model that CODASYL standardized
Very fast record navigation on the hardware of its era
Direct ancestor of IDMS, which still runs large mainframe workloads
weaknesses: Obsolete; no available implementation or hardware
Programs had to navigate pointers by hand, coupling code to physical layout
No declarative query language; the motivation for Codd's relational model
useCases: Studying the origins of database management systems
Teaching the navigational/network model and why relational replaced it
Understanding the lineage of IDMS and CODASYL databases
